C1.text: The actual split of chores explains only a small part of the variation in a partner's perceived fairness.
C1.reading: Supported in direction: the split's own share of a partner's perceived fairness is about 3% to 11% in the best figures (Sánchez adjusted R² .03; Grote at most 11%), up to about 22% unadjusted in one study, and whole models reach only .05 to .19; the larger figures come from models of cognitions.

C2.text: Comparison referents predict a partner's perceived fairness after the actual split is accounted for.
C2.reading: Weakly and inconsistently supported: referent effects net of the split appear for male referents in two single studies (Italian, Mikula 2009) and are null for female referents, and the prospective data in Grote's panel do not show comparison driving perceived fairness.

C3.text: The justifications a partner accepts for an unequal split predict that partner's perceived fairness after the actual split is accounted for.
C3.reading: Open: no full-text study measures the justifications a partner accepts and enters them with the split; proxies (the woman's paid hours, income in a vignette experiment judged by third parties) predict fairness, and procedural voice predicts it net of the split.

C4.text: A partner's perceived fairness is more strongly associated with that partner's relationship satisfaction than the actual split is.
C4.reading: Probably true on average for women, with exceptions by group and for men; no study compares perceived fairness and the split on a common scale, and the nine papers read in pass 3 add no direct test.

C5.text: The association between the actual split and relationship satisfaction is mediated by perceived fairness.
C5.reading: Partly supported for women in two dyadic studies; no formal, time-ordered mediation test exists, and the pass-3 papers either omit satisfaction or analyse only the first step.

C6.text: Each partner over-claims their own contribution: the two partners' self-reported shares of chores sum to more than the whole.
C6.reading: Weaker than before: three dyadic studies show a small excess over the whole (about 3 to 7 points, largest for cognitive labour), but the large NSFH matched-couple panel finds over-claiming by husbands only, and two other studies cannot test it.

C7.text: Which chores a partner does predicts that partner's perceived fairness beyond the time the chores take.
C7.reading: Open: the only primary test (Blair & Johnson, wives) finds the husband's hours in female-typed chores predict the wife's perceived fairness net of her total labour, with chore type entangled with time and the chores belonging to the other partner.

C8.text: Studies measure perceived fairness of the division of chores mainly with a single self-report item.
C8.reading: Supported: fourteen of eighteen full-text studies use a single self-report item; the exceptions are composites (Kamo's four-item average, Grote's multi-item index) with low reliability.

C9.text: A partner who is over-benefited by the allocation reports lower relationship satisfaction than a partner in an equitable allocation.
C9.reading: Little evidence, leaning against: Coltrane's review reads the over-benefited partner's perceived fairness and split as typically unrelated to marital satisfaction, and two single studies find no or a small effect; no study tests over-benefit against an equitable allocation cleanly.
